learning_experiences: work with peers to identify place value of digits up to millions using place value apparatus,
work in teams to read numbers up to millions in symbols from number charts/ cards,
read and write numbers up to hundred thousand in words from number charts/ cards,
discuss and read numbers up to millions in symbols from number charts or cards,
discuss with peers and form different numbers by rearranging digits of a number up to 100,000,
discuss in teams and round off numbers up to hundred thousand to the nearest 1,000 from number cards and share with other groups,
multiply a given number by itself and identify the answer as the square of the number,
work out the square root of a given number and recognise the value which when multiplied by itself results in the given number,
play games involving whole number using digital devices or other resources,
create number charts involving number of road users to and from school or home. This will create awareness on the level of congestion of traffic on the road and help to address road safety issues.
key_inquiry_questions: How do we read and write numbers in symbols and in words?
sub_strands.design_notes: Official outcomes a to g read word for word. The ranges are uneven in the design: a and b go up to millions, c and d only up to 100,000, e up to 100,000 rounded to the nearest thousand. Each skill keeps its own outcome's limit. HOREB's earlier list had no 'total value' outcome, so total value sits under outcome a with place value. Outcome h is attitudinal and is not mapped to a skill.

skills.name: Place value of digits up to millions
skills.mastery: Given a whole number up to 9,999,999, the child names the place of any digit (ones to millions), including digits beside zeros, and says which digit is in a named place. Numbers in real settings such as a county population or a school budget.
question_forms: name the place of a digit
which digit is in the given place

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 extends place value from hundreds of thousands to millions.

skills.name: Total value of digits up to millions
skills.mastery: Given a whole number up to 9,999,999 the child gives the total value of a chosen digit (digit times its place) and writes the number in expanded form. The child does not confuse the total value of a digit with its place value.
question_forms: total value of an underlined digit
difference between two digits of the same value
build a number from total values

prerequisites.reason: Total value needs the place first.
Total value up to hundreds of thousands is already known.

skills.name: Write numbers up to millions in symbols
skills.mastery: Given a number said or described in parts (for example 3 million, 45 thousand and 7) the child writes it in symbols with every place filled, using zero as a place holder. Numbers up to 9,999,999.
question_forms: read a number aloud and write it

prerequisites.reason: The groups of three digits after the millions depend on place value.

skills.name: Read and write numbers up to 100,000 in words
skills.mastery: The child writes a number up to 100,000 in words (British spelling, hyphen in twenty-one to ninety-nine) and writes a number given in words in figures. Limit as the design sets it: 100,000.
question_forms: spot the spelling or place mistake

prerequisites.reason: Extends reading and writing in words to 100,000.

skills.name: Order numbers up to 100,000
skills.mastery: The child orders a list of four to five numbers up to 100,000 from smallest to largest and largest to smallest, comparing digit counts first and then place by place from the left. Uses < and > correctly.
question_forms: order real quantities such as crowds or prices

prerequisites.reason: Extends ordering from tens of thousands to 100,000.
Comparison of a pair is the base.

skills.name: Round numbers up to 100,000 to the nearest thousand
skills.mastery: The child rounds any whole number up to 100,000 to the nearest 1,000: looks at the hundreds digit, rounds 500 up, and keeps the answer in thousands (for example 49,500 rounds to 50,000).

prerequisites.reason: Rounding to the nearest thousand starts in Grade 5.

skills.name: Squares of whole numbers up to 100
skills.mastery: The child works out the square of a whole number up to 100 as the number times itself (for example 40 squared is 1,600) and recalls the squares of 1 to 12 from memory. Squares of 13 to 100 are worked out, not recalled.

prerequisites.reason: Squaring a two-digit number is a two-digit by two-digit multiplication.

skills.name: Square roots of perfect squares up to 10,000
skills.mastery: Given a perfect square up to 10,000 the child finds its square root and checks it by squaring. The child can say that a number such as 50 is not a perfect square because no whole number multiplied by itself gives 50.
question_forms: side of a square from its area
is it a perfect square, and why

misconceptions.error: Counts places from the left instead of from the ones, so names the wrong place in numbers with different digit counts.

example.question: In 4,206,315 which place is the digit 2 in?
example.wrong_answer: tens (the second place, counted from the left)

misconceptions.cause: Reads the number like a sentence and numbers the digits in order.
misconceptions.reveals: Name the place of the same digit in two numbers of different length.
misconceptions.help: Write the number on a place value chart from the ones place leftwards.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Skips a zero when naming places, so the digits after it are placed one too low.

example.question: In 3,050,600 which place is the 5 in?
example.wrong_answer: hundred thousands (the zero after the 3 was skipped)

misconceptions.cause: Treats zero as nothing instead of a place holder.
misconceptions.reveals: A number with several zeros and a question about the digit after them.
misconceptions.help: Use a place value chart with an empty column filled with 0.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Gives the place name or the digit when asked for the total value.

example.question: What is the total value of 7 in 4,370,215?

misconceptions.cause: Place value and total value are used as the same thing.
misconceptions.reveals: A total value question where the digit is also the answer.
misconceptions.help: Expand the number: 4,000,000 + 300,000 + 70,000 ... and read off the term.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Writes one zero too many or too few after the digit when working out total value.
misconceptions.cause: Counts zeros in the number instead of the places to the right of the digit.
misconceptions.reveals: Distractors ten times larger and ten times smaller.
misconceptions.help: Count the places to the right of the digit on the chart, then write that many zeros.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Joins the parts as they are said, leaving out the zeros that fill a group of three.
misconceptions.cause: Does not know that each group after the millions needs three digits.
misconceptions.reveals: Parts where the thousands group has fewer than three digits.
misconceptions.help: Write each part in its own column group of a place value chart before joining.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the thousands and the units groups in the wrong order.
misconceptions.cause: Writes the smaller group first because it is smaller.
misconceptions.reveals: An option with the groups swapped.
misconceptions.help: Read the number aloud from the left and tick each group off as it is written.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the hundreds word or the word thousand when reading a five-digit number.

example.question: Write 45,320 in words.
example.correct_answer: forty-five thousand, three hundred and twenty

misconceptions.cause: Reads the digits in pairs.
misconceptions.reveals: Numbers with a hundreds digit and a tens digit.
misconceptions.help: Split the number into thousands and the last three digits, read each, join.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Confuses the teens and the -ty numbers when moving between words and figures.

example.question: Write "thirty thousand and fourteen" in figures.

misconceptions.cause: Mixes fourteen and forty because they sound alike.
misconceptions.reveals: Words with a teen and its -ty partner.
misconceptions.help: Say the word slowly: -teen ends with the digit, -ty ends with a zero.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Orders numbers by their first digit only, ignoring how many digits each has.
misconceptions.cause: Compares from the left without counting digits first.
misconceptions.reveals: A four-digit number with a bigger first digit than a five-digit number.
misconceptions.help: Count the digits first: more digits means a bigger whole number.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Gives the order from largest to smallest when asked for smallest to largest (or the reverse).
misconceptions.cause: Does not read the direction word in the question.
misconceptions.reveals: Items that are marked for the direction.
misconceptions.help: Underline the direction word (ascending, smallest to largest) before ordering.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Always drops the hundreds and lower digits to zero, never rounding up.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks rounding is cutting off the end of the number.
misconceptions.reveals: A number whose hundreds digit is 5 or more.
misconceptions.help: Use a number line between two thousands and ask which end is nearer.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Looks at the tens digit, not the hundreds digit, to decide whether to round up.
misconceptions.cause: Looks at the digit just to the right of the one asked about, taking the wrong place as the one to round to.
misconceptions.reveals: A number where the hundreds digit is under 5 and the tens digit is 5 or more.
misconceptions.help: Circle the thousands digit, then look only at the next digit to its right.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Doubles the number instead of multiplying it by itself.
misconceptions.cause: Reads the small 2 as "times 2".
misconceptions.reveals: The doubled answer as a distractor.
misconceptions.help: Draw a 9 by 9 square of dots and count them.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Squares only the non-zero digit, so the square of a multiple of ten has too few zeros.
misconceptions.cause: Squares 3 and writes the zero back, or squares 3 and forgets the zero.
misconceptions.reveals: Squares of multiples of ten with distractors 9 and 90.
misconceptions.help: Write 30 x 30 as 3 tens x 3 tens = 9 hundreds.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Halves the number instead of finding the number that multiplied by itself gives it.
misconceptions.cause: Confuses square root with half.
misconceptions.reveals: Half of the number as a distractor.
misconceptions.help: Ask "which number times itself is 64?" and test 8 x 8.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Takes the root of a square ending in zeros as ten times too big or too small.
misconceptions.cause: Does not pair the zeros: two zeros in a square become one zero in the root.
misconceptions.reveals: Roots of 400, 900 and 6,400 with distractors ten times larger.
misconceptions.help: Square a few multiples of ten and notice the pattern of zeros.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

learning_experiences: multiply up to a 4-digit number by a 2- digit number using; - fact families - skip counting - multiplication chart - expanded form - digital devices, - estimate products using; - rounding off factors - compatibility of numbers, - make patterns involving multiplication with products not exceeding 1,000 using number cards, - work with peers and play games involving multiplication using digital devices or other resources such as number cards.
key_inquiry_questions: How do we multiply numbers?
sub_strands.design_notes: Outcome a goes up to a 4-digit number by a 2-digit number. Outcome b rounds both numbers to the nearest ten (not the nearest ten and then the nearest hundred). Outcome c patterns use numbers not exceeding 1,000. Outcome d is attitudinal and not mapped.

outcomes.text: multiply up to a 4-digit number by a 2-digit number in real-life situations

skills.name: Multiply a 4-digit number by a 2-digit number
skills.mastery: The child multiplies a number up to 4 digits by a 2-digit number by the standard written method (two partial products, with zero placed in the ones of the tens row) or by partitioning, and solves a story that needs it. Products below 1,000,000.
question_forms: spot the mistake in a partial product

prerequisites.reason: The same method with one more digit.

skills.name: Estimate products by rounding to the nearest ten
skills.mastery: The child rounds both numbers to the nearest ten, multiplies the rounded numbers, and says whether an exact answer is sensible. Rounding to the nearest ten for both factors, as outcome b says.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 estimates a product by rounding to the nearest ten.

skills.name: Make and continue multiplication patterns (numbers up to 1,000)
skills.mastery: The child finds the rule of a pattern made by multiplying (for example times 2 or times 3), continues it, and finds a missing term. Terms do not exceed 1,000.
question_forms: find the rule from a table

misconceptions.error: Forgets the zero in the ones place when multiplying by the tens digit, so the second partial product is ten times too small.

example.question: 2,314 x 23
example.wrong_answer: 11,570 (the row for the 2 tens was not shifted: 6,942 + 4,628)

misconceptions.cause: Does not remember that the 2 in 23 stands for 20.
misconceptions.reveals: Distractor with the second row shifted wrongly.
misconceptions.help: Multiply by 3, then by 20 (write the zero first), then add.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds the carried digit before multiplying, or forgets it, in a long product.
misconceptions.cause: Carries are held in the head and lost.
misconceptions.help: Write the carries small above the next digit and cross each one off when used.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Multiplies only by the ones digit of the two-digit number.
misconceptions.cause: Treats a 2-digit multiplier as a 1-digit one.
misconceptions.reveals: Answer equal to the product by the ones digit.
misconceptions.help: Break 15 into 10 + 5 and compute both parts.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Rounds only one of the two factors, so the estimate is not the usual one.
misconceptions.cause: Thinks rounding one is enough.
misconceptions.reveals: Distractor from rounding only one factor.
misconceptions.help: Rewrite the question with both numbers rounded before multiplying.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Loses a zero when multiplying the rounded tens, so the estimate is ten times too small.
misconceptions.cause: Multiplies 28 x 7 and does not put back both zeros.
misconceptions.reveals: Estimate with one zero too few.
misconceptions.help: Count the zeros in both factors and put the same number on the answer.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Finds an additive rule (the difference between the first two terms) for a multiplying pattern.
misconceptions.cause: Looks at the difference between terms only.
misconceptions.reveals: Pattern that grows by a growing amount.
misconceptions.help: Divide each term by the one before it and see whether the answer stays the same.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Expects the gap between terms to stay the same, so continues a doubling pattern by repeating the last gap.
misconceptions.cause: Has met adding patterns more often than multiplying ones.
misconceptions.reveals: Next term from repeating the last gap.
misconceptions.help: Write the multiplier above each arrow between the terms.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

learning_experiences: - divide up to a 4-digit number by up to a 3-digit number and share the answers where the dividend is greater than the divisor using;
- relationship between multiplication and division - long method,
- work out quotients by rounding off the dividend and divisor to the nearest ten,
- work out questions involving two, three or four operations up to 3-digit numbers,
- divide whole numbers using digital devices or other resources.
key_inquiry_questions: Where is division used in real life?
sub_strands.design_notes: Outcome a: a dividend of up to 4 digits by a divisor of up to 3 digits, with the dividend greater than the divisor. The design does not ask for remainders in decimals; remainders are kept as whole-number remainders. Outcome c, combined operations, is up to 3-digit numbers (HOREB's G6_BODMAS_BASIC is Grade 5 and stays there). Outcome d is attitudinal and not mapped.

outcomes.text: divide up to a 4-digit number by up to a 3-digit number where the dividend is greater than the divisor in real -life situations

skills.name: Divide up to a 4-digit number by up to a 3-digit number
skills.mastery: The child divides a 4-digit number by a 1-, 2- or 3-digit number by long division, with the dividend greater than the divisor, gives any remainder as a whole number, and checks by multiplying back and adding the remainder.
question_forms: spot the mistake in the working

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 extends the dividend to 4 digits and the divisor to 3.

skills.name: Estimate quotients by rounding to the nearest ten
skills.mastery: The child rounds the dividend and divisor to the nearest ten, divides the rounded numbers, and uses the estimate to check that an exact answer is sensible.

prerequisites.reason: The same idea at a smaller size.

skills.name: Combined operations with the four operations (up to 3-digit numbers)
skills.mastery: The child works out an expression with two or three of the four operations, doing multiplication and division before addition and subtraction and working left to right within each level, with numbers up to 3 digits. Brackets are taken first where they appear.
question_forms: spot the step done in the wrong order

prerequisites.reason: Order of operations is introduced in Grade 5.

misconceptions.error: Leaves a zero out of the quotient when a digit of the dividend is too small to divide.
misconceptions.cause: Brings down the next digit and forgets to write 0 in the answer.
misconceptions.help: Write a 0 in the answer each time a digit cannot be divided.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the remainder as another digit of the quotient or drops it.

example.wrong_answer: 834 (the remainder 4 written as a digit of the answer)

misconceptions.cause: Does not know what to do with the leftover.
misconceptions.help: Check by multiplying back and adding the remainder; it must match the dividend.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Divides the smaller digit by the larger divisor part the wrong way round (for example 4 by 12 as 12 by 4).

example.question: First step of 4,536 / 12
example.wrong_answer: 12 / 4 = 3 (the divisor divided by the first digit)

misconceptions.cause: Swaps dividend and divisor when the first digit is smaller.
misconceptions.reveals: Working showing a swapped first step.
misconceptions.help: Use the first digits that make a number at least as big as the divisor.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Rounds the dividend but not the divisor, so the estimate is awkward and usually wrong.
misconceptions.cause: Rounds one number only.
misconceptions.help: Round both numbers, then divide the rounded numbers.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Cancels zeros unevenly when dividing rounded numbers, giving an estimate ten times too large or small.
misconceptions.cause: Crosses a zero off the top only.
misconceptions.help: Cross the same number of zeros off the dividend and the divisor.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Works strictly from left to right whatever the operations are.
misconceptions.cause: Reads a sum like a sentence.
misconceptions.reveals: Expression where the left-to-right answer differs.
misconceptions.help: Ask which operation must be done first and underline it.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Always multiplies before dividing, even when the division comes first.
misconceptions.cause: Believes multiplication ranks above division.
misconceptions.reveals: Expression with division written before multiplication.
misconceptions.help: Work multiplication and division in the order they appear, left to right.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Ignores the brackets and works the line in the order written.
misconceptions.cause: Reads brackets as decoration.
misconceptions.reveals: Expression with brackets whose left-to-right value differs.
misconceptions.help: Do what is inside the brackets first; draw a box round it.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Subtracts before multiplying when the subtraction comes first in the line.
misconceptions.cause: Does the first operation written.
misconceptions.reveals: The left-to-right answer as a distractor.
misconceptions.help: Do the multiplication first; use brackets to show the other reading.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

learning_experiences: identify LCM of numbers given from number cards,
add and subtract fractions using LCM by listing multiples,
add and subtract mixed fractions by converting the fractions to improper fractions,
add and subtract mixed fractions by adding and subtracting whole number and fraction parts separately,
list the inverse of numbers between 1 and 10,

calculate the reciprocal of a number by dividing 1 (one) by the number. Always start by working out the reciprocal of whole numbers before solving the reciprocal of proper fractions up to a 2- digit number,
discuss the various reciprocals of a proper fraction,
calculate squares of fractions through multiplication or practically,
change fractions to equivalent fractions with denominator 100 through multiplication,
identify a percentage as a fraction with denominator 100,
work with peers on how to change fractions to percentages and vice versa,
play digital games involving fractions.
key_inquiry_questions: How do we add or subtract fractions?
Where is percentage used in day-to-day life?
sub_strands.design_notes: Official outcomes a to h (i is attitudinal). HOREB's earlier list joined add and subtract fractions under one letter and add and subtract mixed numbers under one letter; the design has them separate (a, b and c, d), and percentages are g (fraction to percentage) and h (percentage to fraction). Outcome f (squares of fractions) is 'kicd_read': the design's text was not fully clear, and a person should confirm the limit (numerator 1 digit, denominator up to 2 digits). Outcome e (reciprocal) is of proper fractions only.

skills.name: Add fractions with unlike denominators using the LCM
skills.mastery: The child finds the LCM of two denominators (each up to 12), renames both fractions with it, adds the numerators, keeps the denominator, and simplifies. Sums that exceed 1 are written as a mixed number.
question_forms: add two fractions in a story
why we need a common denominator

prerequisites.reason: Adding like fractions is the last step.
Renaming with the LCM uses equivalent fractions.
The common denominator is the LCM.

skills.name: Subtract fractions with unlike denominators using the LCM
skills.mastery: The child renames two unlike fractions with the LCM of their denominators (each up to 12), subtracts the numerators, keeps the denominator, and simplifies. The first fraction is larger.

prerequisites.reason: Subtracting like fractions is the last step.

skills.name: Add mixed numbers
skills.mastery: The child adds two mixed numbers by adding the wholes and the fractions separately (using the LCM when the denominators differ) or by changing to improper fractions, and writes the answer in simplest form, renaming when the fractions total more than 1.
question_forms: change a mixed number to an improper fraction
spot the mistake in the conversion

prerequisites.reason: Renaming when the fractions total more than one.

skills.name: Subtract mixed numbers
skills.mastery: The child subtracts one mixed number from a larger one, including the case where the fraction part is too small and one whole must be renamed, and gives the answer in simplest form.
question_forms: spot the mistake when the fraction is too small

prerequisites.reason: Same structure of whole and fraction parts.
Renaming one whole as a fraction.

skills.name: Reciprocal of a proper fraction
skills.mastery: The child writes the reciprocal of a proper fraction whose numerator and denominator are up to 2 digits by turning it upside down, and knows that a number times its reciprocal is 1.
question_forms: why has a whole number no reciprocal fraction written 0

prerequisites.reason: Understanding a fraction as numerator over denominator.

skills.name: Square of a fraction
skills.mastery: The child squares a fraction with a one-digit numerator and a denominator of up to 2 digits by squaring the numerator and the denominator, and writes the answer in simplest form.
question_forms: story about area of a square cloth

prerequisites.reason: Squares of the numerator and denominator.

skills.name: Express a fraction as a percentage
skills.mastery: The child writes a fraction as a percentage by making the denominator 100 or by dividing and multiplying by 100, including fractions with denominators that are factors of 100 and a mark out of a total.
question_forms: write a score as a percentage
which fraction is the larger percentage

prerequisites.reason: Making the denominator 100 is an equivalent fraction.

skills.name: Convert a percentage to a fraction
skills.mastery: The child writes a percentage as a fraction out of 100 and simplifies it to simplest form.

misconceptions.error: Adds the numerators and the denominators.
misconceptions.cause: Treats the fraction bar like a separator between two whole numbers.
misconceptions.reveals: The across answer as a distractor.
misconceptions.help: Shade 1/2 and 1/3 of the same bar and show the total is more than 1/2, not 2/5.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the product of the denominators instead of the LCM, so the answer is correct but not in simplest form, or the child stops early.
misconceptions.cause: Does not look for the smallest common multiple.
misconceptions.reveals: Answer correct in value but not simplest form.
misconceptions.help: List multiples of both denominators and choose the smallest shared one.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Changes the denominator to the common one but leaves the numerator.
misconceptions.cause: Remembers "make the bottoms the same" but not "and multiply the top too".
misconceptions.help: Multiply top and bottom by the same number every time.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Subtracts numerators and subtracts denominators.
misconceptions.cause: Same across-method as adding.
misconceptions.help: Rename with the LCM first, then subtract only the numerators.
misconceptions.source: a familiar error type in maths education (no single source cited); how often Kenyan learners make it is to be confirmed by a teacher

misconceptions.error: Subtracts the numerators without first renaming the second fraction with the common denominator.
misconceptions.cause: Subtracts without renaming first.
misconceptions.help: Rename both fractions with the common denominator before subtracting.
misconceptions.source: to be confirmed by a teacher (no source yet)

misconceptions.error: Adds the wholes and the fractions but leaves an improper fraction in the answer or drops the extra whole.
misconceptions.cause: Does not rename 5/4 as 1 1/4.

skills.name: Identify decimals up to ten-thousandths
skills.mastery: The child names the place of a digit after the decimal point up to ten-thousandths, gives its value as a fraction, and writes a decimal from a place description (for example 7 ten-thousandths as 0.0007).
question_forms: write the decimal from its words

prerequisites.reason: Extends place names from thousandths to ten-thousandths.

skills.name: Round decimals to up to 3 decimal places
skills.mastery: The child rounds a decimal to 1, 2 or 3 decimal places by looking at the next digit, including when the rounding carries across a 9 (for example 4.9996 to 3 places is 5.000).

prerequisites.reason: The rounding rule is the same.

skills.name: Convert decimals to fractions
skills.mastery: The child writes a decimal with up to 3 places as a fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1,000 and simplifies it.

prerequisites.reason: The denominator comes from the last place.

skills.name: Convert fractions to decimals
skills.mastery: The child writes a fraction as a decimal by dividing the numerator by the denominator or by renaming it with denominator 10, 100 or 1,000 (denominators such as 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 20, 25, 50).

skills.name: Convert decimals to percentages
skills.mastery: The child writes a decimal as a percentage by multiplying by 100 (moving the point two places), including decimals less than 0.1 and more than 1.
question_forms: story about a tank or a score

prerequisites.reason: A percentage is a fraction out of 100.

skills.name: Convert percentages to decimals
skills.mastery: The child writes a percentage as a decimal by dividing by 100 (moving the point two places left), including 5%, 0.5% and 120%.

skills.name: Add decimals up to 4 decimal places

prerequisites.reason: Adding decimals with different numbers of places.

skills.name: Subtract decimals up to 4 decimal places
skills.mastery: The child subtracts one decimal from another with up to 4 decimal places in columns with the points in line, renaming across zeros and filling empty places with zeros.
